utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom and those just around assisting us. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue the examination of the present witness, I would like to turn into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. May I take it there are no other procedural matters to be discussed at this moment. Therefore, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to save time, Your Honour, while the witness is coming up in, if I could have the Registrar to bring up P2604, at page 38. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bajic. Mr. Bajic, may I remind you that the solemn declaration you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony is still binding you. That is, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson will now continue her cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Bajic. Mr. Bajic, I had just one additional question on the KT register that we were looking at yesterday that I neglected to ask at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could look at the second entry on this page, which is entry 796.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is one of the ones we looked at yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could then go to the next page of the register where this entry continues.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you can see under column 32 it refers -- that column entry states: "Judgement or first instance decision." And that entry has a date of 6 December 1996 and refers to a transfer of this case file to the municipal prosecutor's office in Knin. And I'd just like to confirm with that you this entry refers to a transfer related to the termination of the Military Prosecutor's Office at that time, in December of 1996, and the transfer of all existing case files from the Split Military Prosecutor's Offices -- office to civilian prosecutor's offices. Is that a correct understanding of that entry?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 6th of December, 1996, military courts and Military Prosecutor's Offices were abolished, and all pending cases, or cases where final decisions had not been taken, were referred to the regular prosecutor's offices. The cases where final decisions were taken were filed in the Split county prosecutor' office where they can still be found today. Thus, this particular file was referred to the Zadar prosecutor's office on the 6th of December, and bears this particular reference number that we have here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And in contrast to this transfer of all the files in December of 1996, if a case was referred to a civilian prosecutor's office in circumstances where the suspect had been demobilised before the indictment was issued or in circumstances where it was discovered that the suspect was not a HV member, that would be entered in column 26 on this chart, where it says: "Deferred to other public prosecutor's office." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on to another topic now which is the duty that you referred to yesterday of commanders to file criminal reports. And you testified yesterday about a general duty imposed on all members of state institutions to file criminal reports when they become aware of a crime. And I'd like to ask you a few more specific questions about the duties of commanders in the Croatian army in relation to the conduct of their subordinates. And my first question is: You testified yesterday that you're not a professional soldier. Do you have any specialised knowledge or training in the duties of Croatian army commanders, vis-a-vis the conduct of their subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not a professional soldier, and I didn't attend any sort of training. My answer had to do with the general provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure, i.e., Article 141 of the law of the time, which provides for all public authority bodies and all state institutions and their duty to report to the law enforcement agencies of all the criminal offences they become aware of, including commanders of units.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to Exhibit P1007, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday, you were asked questions about criminal versus disciplinary proceedings and you explained that criminal procedures are quite distinct from disciplinary procedures, and you said that Military Prosecutor's Offices and military courts had nothing to do with disciplinary procedures. And --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- in light of the fact that you've given evidence that these are two distinct systems, I'd like to ask you, again, whether have you any specialised knowledge or training in the structure or operation of the system of military discipline that was in place at the time of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I have no other knowledge than the general knowledge a lawyer would have.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we go to page 2 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, if I could direct your attention to Article 3 of this law.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could move to the next page in the English. I'm particularly interested in point 7, under Article 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you can see that, according to this Article, violations of the Code of Military Discipline include commission of a crime for which proceedings are initiated ex officio.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 10 in the English and page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If you could look at Article 31, paragraph 1, where it says: "In situations where the authorised officer finds that the offence against military discipline is also a criminal offence, the case shall be sent via regular channels to the authorised prosecutor; if he thinks that it is in the interest of the service, he shall also initiate disciplinary procedures." Now, you were asked yesterday about the possibilities of parallel investigations by military commander and by the military police, and those questions were not very specific as to the type of investigation involved. Would you agree, as indicated by these Articles of the Military Discipline Code that a commander can conduct disciplinary proceedings in parallel to a criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I said so myself yesterday that criminal procedure or criminal proceedings are quite distinct from military disciplinary proceedings, and I spoke of the criminal proceedings yesterday. In other words, yes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like to move on to another topic briefly. You were asked questioned yesterday about the case-load of the Military Prosecutor's Office. And my question is simply this: To your knowledge, did the Split military prosecutor ever drop a case or fail to indict or prosecute a case because it was too busy to do so?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm glad that you put the question to me. I'd like to dispel any possible doubts about the conduct of Military Prosecutor's Offices. I tried to explain this yesterday, and I should clarify it today. All criminal reports, absolutely all criminal reports filed before military prosecutor in the Military Prosecutor's Office in Split either against known or unknown persons, were received by us, registered in the register and processed. The fact that there were five or six military prosecutors and deputies did not have a bearing on either the quality of their work or on the fate of these cases, whether they would be closed or not. They were processed according to the pace when they were received, and all those that were not processed by 6th December, 1996, were specified and referred to regular prosecutor's offices, and they were all brought to a close, according to the prescribed procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, based on our analysis of the KT register, during August and September 1995, the Split military prosecutor received a total of five reports against known perpetrators that are relevant to the indictment in this case; and that's basically, as I said yesterday, looting, destruction, and killings in a number of municipalities in Sector South during August and September. And these are four cases of aggravated theft and one murder case. And more generally, our analysis of the same register, up until the end of March 1996, indicates a total of 31 reports relevant to the indictment in this case. Two are for murder, one is for robbery and the rest are theft cases. And there are, in addition, 18 other criminal reports that relate to looting in the liberated area after Operation Storm but they're outside the scope of this indictment, either because of the time that they were committed or the location. And when you were asked about the number of reports related to this indictment received in August in your interview with the Prosecution, you stated that the number of crimes committed was actually much larger - this is at paragraph 7 of your statement to the Prosecution - but you noted that reports were also filed with civilian prosecutor's offices, and you added that it was your recollection that most of the crimes were committed in September, October, and November; but I said you didn't analyse this yourself but that reports on this were being submitted through the Ministry of Justice's offices for cooperation with the ICTY. So I'd just like to clarify that answer about your information on the number of crimes that were committed at different times. Is it right that your understanding that most of the crimes were committed in September, October, and November is based primarily on reports that Croatia has sent to the ICTY; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I said under item 7 in my discussions with you when you were in Zagreb and what I said yesterday is something that I confirmed, this is my view of the matter. The material that you presented which is based on the archives of the Military Prosecutor's Office in Split is absolutely correct and accurate. My understanding of the situation at the time when I was deputy military prosecutor in Split was that most of the documents at the time were filed before regular -- regular prosecutor offices in Sibenik, Sinj, Zadar, and Split. I was aware of the actual figures only at a later date based on the information that the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Croatia produced in late 1995 when they -- when the ministry asked the prosecutor's offices to report to the ministry on a regular basis on all the matters related to Operation Storm. I recalled that in 2003 an analysis of the cases of the sort was compiled, containing cases of all the prosecutor's offices from Zadar, Sibenik, Split, Dubrovnik, and beyond. The analysis was sent to the Ministry of Justice with a view to disseminating it to the international community. The information contained therein --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bajic. I -- I actually wasn't looking for all the details. I appreciate your thorough answer but I just wanted to understand the nature of the information that you were basing your answer on. And I understand that it is based on reports on investigations and prosecutions that were conducted, so I understand that your conclusion that most of the crimes were committed in September, October, and November, is based on statistics on the number of investigations and prosecutions.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And another thing you were asked about yesterday was how frequently it occurred that a person would be suspected of being in the HV because they were wearing a military uniform, and after further investigation, it was established that the person was, in fact, not a member of the HV. And you testified that such situations occurred quite frequently in the aftermath of Operation Storm, "According to the information I had at the time, a large number of members of the Croatian army were demobilised." And you added that: "While acting upon a certain criminal report, we established that the person reported was no longer a member of the Croatian army." My question is this: Your conclusion that these situations occurred quite frequently, is that conclusion based on the number of criminal reports received by the Split military prosecutor that were then deferred to municipal Prosecutors when it was discovered the suspect was not a HV member?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, partly on this sort of personal knowledge, and partly on the fact that it was a well-known fact that after Operation Storm, a great many members of the reserve forces were demobilised. For this reason, all or most of the reports for Operation Storm were forwarded to regular prosecutor's offices. Furthermore, based on the information published in 2003, which stated roughly that 4122 -- eight -- persons were entered into KT registers of regular and military prosecutors and 2262 persons were entered into the registers for persons unknown, led me to the conclusion that most of the persons reported had, in the meantime, become civilians and lost their status of HV members.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In relation to the reports received by civilian prosecutors, you don't have any specific information as to how many of those reports involved civilians dressed in military uniforms, do you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any specific indicators. What I know from personal knowledge is that my office, at the time when I was the prosecutor and in 1996, when these cases were being processed, on the -- there was a colleague from the Split municipal prosecutor's office in my building and they consulted me on how these decisions and indictments should be formulated. From these numerous contacts, I received additional information to the statistics that I referred to a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, of the 49 criminal reports in the KT register that relate to the crimes of burning, looting, or killing after Operation Storm in the liberated area, 19 of them indicate, according to the register, that they were deferred to municipal prosecutors. And as you testified yesterday, these cases could have been deferred either because it was discovered that the person was not a HV member at the time of the crime, or because the person ceased to be a HV member before being indicted. So the concrete information that you base your conclusion about civilians in uniform on, would that concrete information be some portion of these 19 reports that were deferred to municipal prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you with certainly where I got the information from, whether it was from the cases themselves, or from conversations with my colleagues, fellow prosecutors, who worked on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could move now to 65 ter 7374.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bajic, this is the first tab in the bundle of case files that I gave you yesterday, if you want to refer to the hard copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just get some clarification while switch to go a new topic. I'm not sure I followed counsel's question at page 7, lines 13 through 15, that there were only a total of five reports against known perpetrators in the KT register.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think I clarified that that was in August and September. Reports received in August and September. That was my --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Reports received but not for crimes committed in August and September.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This being clarified, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This case, Mr. Bajic, relates to entry KT 989 in the register, and it's -- is the conviction of two HV members for looting in Knin on the 31st of August, and in that case they were stopped by the MP at the Knin train station. Did you have an opportunity to look at this case overnight?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 8 in the English and page 7 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the -- around the middle of the page it says -- it refers to the defence of Marinko Sabljic, and according to his defence, he said: "Upon their arrival in Knin Petar Vujnovac remained in a cafe to have a drink there, while himself and Grubicic continued driving through the town and they saw many trucks and soldiers near some houses loading various objects on to those trucks." And if we move to the next page in the English at the bottom, it's the same page in the B/C/S and it refers to the defence of Damir Grubisic. And he says: "In the vicinity of the spot where they wanted to park the vehicle, they saw some members of the HV taking various items from the houses and loading them on to the trucks; it was right there that one Croatian soldier asked them to transport for him some of those items that were scattered in front of the houses to the railway station which they accepted and loaded onto the truck ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could look at another case now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm just going to point you to a few items, and I will ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 7375.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this relates to entry KT 997 in the register. And it is the conviction of a member of the 113th Brigade for looting in the village of Kosovo on the 2nd of September, 1995. And the case file indicates he was indicted on the 11th of November, 1995, and the judgement rendered on 1st of February, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we go to page 5 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At the top of the page in the English, it indicates that since he's -- since the time of his indictment, the soldier in question has now become an active member of the 72nd Military Police Battalion Company in Sibenik. And a little bit further down on the page in English, the bottom of the large paragraph the court says: "Moreover, the reasons for the commission of this crime given by the accused in his defence are not acceptable, because the commission of such crimes must not be a rule for somebody to obtain some item that he or she may need, nor may there be a justification in the fact that everybody is 'loading and carrying things off, so why not me?'."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to 65 ter 7376, which is the third tab in your bundle. And this case is KT 1000. It relates to the conviction of a number of members of the 204th Brigade for looting in Golubic on the 8th of September, 1995. And if we go to page 10 in the English and the seventh page in the B/C/S. And at the beginning of the English it says: "From the defence of the first accused Davor Zdrilic, it follows that at the time of the commission of the charged crime he was a member of the Croatian army, that is, they were in the Golubic area together with young conscripts where there was the command of the 204th Brigade of the HV. It has also been mentioned that in front of the command the conscripts were loading various household items onto the trucks, which he assumes were probably brought there by somebody." And if we could move down to the middle of the page in the English and to the next page in the B/C/S. This refers to the defence of the second accused and it says: "He stated in his defence that at the time he was a member of the Croatian army at the guard post above Golubic and that he, after his shift, came to Golubic and near the command saw a truck that had already been loaded with various items, and since he wanted to go to Zadar, he asked them to drive [sic] him to Zadar." And if we could go to page 13 in the English and, again, the next page in the B/C/S. Near the bottom in English and in the middle in the B/C/S it states that the sixth accused Vlade Lukic states in his defence that on the charged event they were in the position in the Golubic area that is, that he was this charge of communications and that he remembers that items required for the units were at that time taken from that area. As for the charged event itself, he remembers that he loaded the tools for himself onto the truck, but since it was already dark he cannot recall whether anybody else loaded anything and which items they were; however, he remembers that the commander allowed them to take the truck to transport the items and that they can go home with it. And if we go to the next page in the English and the next page in the B/C/S. And it's near the bottom in the English and at the top in the B/C/S. And it says: "The witness Miodrag Pavic has pointed out in his testimony that on the charged event 15 of them, military conscripts, were loading the items listed in the indictment onto the truck under the order probably given by the battery commander and that two of them, namely, himself and Stipe Vulic, who were both conscripts, were designated to escort the truck; however, he knew neither where they were going nor whom the said items were for."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, having read these files and based on your experience as a prosecutor and as a military prosecutor at the time of these events, would you agree that these cases contain indications, and I'm referring specifically to indications such as large group of HV soldiers loading looted items onto trucks in Knin, a soldier under indictment for theft becoming a member of the 72nd Military Police Battalion and a large group of conscripts loading looted items onto a truck in front of their unit command. Do these indications indicate to that you looting was, to some extent, accepted or permitted within the HV units at the time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with your conclusion. Besides, it is a fact that I have to reiterate, that all reports of criminal offences submitted to state prosecutors were processed, but the problem did not lie with military prosecutor's cases but the cases which went unreported. Your conclusions are valid. I concur with the conclusion that this was a phenomenon which can be read in the explanations to the judgements from testimonies of witnesses and opinions of judges and, indeed, such cases were numerous in other -- in regular prosecutor's offices because of the change of status of perpetrators. Yes, I do agree with all you've said.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one minor question. On this last case, this judgement was rendered on the 5th of November, 1998 and that was, of course, after the Law on Amnesty was passed. And in your evidence yesterday you stated that the amnesty law related to acts that had something to do with aggression, armed rebellion, or armed conflict. And I would just like to clarify with you that the amnesty law was not applicable and that it did not amnesty crime such as burning, looting, or killing committed after Operation Storm; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. In the text of the general amnesty law dated 1996, it reads that the Law on General Amnesty shall apply only to persons who committed their offences in connection with the war but it shall not be applied to war crimes or criminal offences against international humanitarian law, et cetera. So in this case, when it concerns looting, robbery, theft, arson committed after the operation or during the operation, the Law on General Amnesty was not applied. This was not the goal and the purpose of that law.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender these three case files, 65 ter 7374 through 7376, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 7374 becomes Exhibit P2608; 65 ter number 7376 becomes Exhibit P2609; and 65 ter number 7376 becomes Exhibit P2610.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. P2608, P2609, and P2610 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could move now to D1619, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, could I ask one point, clarification. Mr. Bajic, you said, yes, these crimes were not exempted from prosecution because the Law on Amnesty did not apply. And you gave two categories; the first is that the crimes, in order to be covered by the Law on Amnesty should be crimes committed in connection with the war, and, at the same time, they should not be war crimes or violations of international humanitarian law. Now, the categories here, were they not covered by the Law on Amnesty because they were violations of international humanitarian law, or were they not covered by the Law on Amnesty because they were not linked anymore to the armed conflict? Which of the two would apply here? Is it the time-frame; or is it the character of the crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The criminal offences that we discussed through those three documents could not be exempted pursuant to the general amnesty law because they were not committed in connection with the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, in front of you is an invitation on the screen dated 27 September 1995 to, among other individuals, all military prosecutors, and it's an invitation to a joint working session on 19 October 1995. Do you recall whether you attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not attend it because this invitation did address all military prosecutors. I was a deputy military prosecutor. I believe that there were four or five military prosecutors in general. Apart from that in Split, there was one in Karlovac, Zagreb, Osijek, Rijeka, et cetera. And this invitation was addressed to them. Deputy military prosecutors did not attend, because the invitation did not involve them, so I did not attend the meeting myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And the subject, according to this invitation, is for the purpose of ensuring efficient prevention and removal of the observed faults and punishable acts in the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia. And for the purpose of ensuring lawful and regular operation of the bodies of the Ministry of Defence, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to D1621.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I understand you weren't at this meeting, but I would like you to show you the conclusions from that meeting and ask you if you can assist the Court, based on the knowledge that you have from the working office. And I'd like to direct your attention, in particular, to items 6 and 7 where it says: "The Ministry of Defence shall commit commands of the units of the armed forces ... to act in accordance with the law regarding serving of court summons to members of the armed forces ..." And: "The Ministry of Defence shall commit units, the Main Staff, and the commands of the Military Districts to meet the court requests fully in a timely manner. Also regarding the submission of necessary evidence for specific cases," et cetera. And my question is: Based on your experience in the Military Prosecutor's Office in Split, did you have problems with the HV units and Military District Command in serving court summons and having them meet court requests fully and in a timely manner? And I'm talking about the time-period after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Object as to foundation, how this witness would know whether the court was having problems serving summons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do not see serving summons specifically mentioned here. Apart from that, let's hear the answer of the witness and let's find out what the basis of his knowledge is. Could you please answer the question, Mr. Bajic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At working meetings such as this was, what was discussed was how to make the operations of military prosecutors and military courts as effective and expedient as possible. Because of frequent change of address and stations of different military personnel and military units, there was -- there were problems in speedy communication in requests of certain documents and in the -- in the service of summons because we could -- we often had to postpone hearings because soldiers did not heed summons, so I can see that military prosecutors and military judges sought assistance at such a meeting as this one, was based on their experience. This is how I see the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did you personally encounter instances where hearings you were involved in had to be postponed because soldiers didn't heed the summons?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such occasions. There were such occasions. As I say, the problem was the service of process, addresses, and failure to appear before court but that was particularly problematic in 1991, 1992, due to lack of respect to military justice system. But things improved subsequently. Those conclusions that we can see concern assistance sought from the Ministry of Defence to help the processes that Ministry of Justice was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to turn to ask you a few questions to follow up on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, sorry to interrupt you. You read paragraph 7 to the witness, which seems to deal primarily with obtaining evidence, but you focussed your question on the -- the serving of court summons, which seems to be the subject matter of paragraph 6. I'm a bit confused by this --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was following up on an answer the witness had given about problems serving summons, and I was just asking him if he had personally experienced these problems. It was follow up to his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, I would like to ask you now a few questions about the evidence you gave on the role of the military police in preventing and detecting perpetrators of criminal offences. And in particular in your statement to the Defence at question 14 you said: "After determining that a criminal offence has been committed, the criminal" -- sorry, "The civilian police conducts criminal processing of the case." And you said: "In the course of the processing of the case it would be established that the perpetrator was a member of the military, the military police would then take over the criminal processing." And yesterday you expanded on than a little bit, and you -- in particular when you were asked who had jurisdiction to begin an investigation into an incident where it is reported that unnamed members of the Croatian army were in the vicinity of houses that are on fire, your answer was: "You see, it is dubious on the basis of what you asked me, whether there are sufficient grounds to suspect that those members of the HV perpetrated that criminal offence or the perpetrators were completely unknown and possibly civilians. But regardless of that, in such a situation, forces of law, as the law states, have to undertake all the possible and necessary measures to secure evidence and to conduct inquiries or pre-criminal investigation and in such a case, both the civilian police and the military police, whichever is closer to the scene, should do something; or if the perpetrators are unknown, then bodies of general jurisdiction would have primacy, which means civilian police, and if there's grounds to suspect that the perpetrators are military personnel, then the military police would be duty-bound to act." I would just like to look at a couple of more concrete examples which are contained in P886.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is the duty service log-book of the Knin military police company.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 4 of the B/C/S and the first page of the second English translation attached to this document. And this is the page for 11th of August. If we could look at the entry for 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And according to this entry, information is received from the 40th Engineers Company, reporting shooting and arson in Kovacic hamlet. And in the last column the remarks say that Cobra 40 patrol, which is a military police patrol, is sent; report attached.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 16 in the English and page 16 in the B/C/S. This is an entry from the 23rd of August. If we could look at the entry for 8.10, which, I believe, is the first one.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is information received from the Knin police administration that some 100 metres from the police check-point at the exit for Grude after a fire, a detonation took place, and it is assumed that a HV member set fire to a house. And the remarks say that: "A patrol sent, Mosor 31 ... at the scene no one was found." And it says: "No HV members were seen to be burning houses."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 22 in the English and page 20 in the B/C/S. This is a report from the 26th of August, and I'm looking at the entry under 1641, which is number 6. This is a report from Ivan Peric, civilian, owner of the house in Lukar. And it says: "Slavko Peric, HV, is threatening him and his son Tomislav in Lukar ... and a patrol was dispatched but did not find the HV on the scene." And finally, if we could look at entry on page 55 in the English and page 38 in the B/C/S. And this is from the 9th of September. And if we look at the entry under 2010, number 1. And this is report from the Knin police administration that, on the road towards Stara Straza, uniformed persons have been observed setting houses on fire. And under the remarks it says: "As it is dark, it is better that the patrols go out tomorrow."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And my question is: The entries we just looked where the Knin military police company is receiving reports of possible crimes by HV members and sending patrols or, at least in that last case, deciding to send a patrol the next day, would you agree that these are examples where there are grounds to suspect that the perpetrators are military personnel and, as a result, the military police is responding to these incidents?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And yesterday you were asked about what a HV commander should do if he has information that a crime has been committed, and you were asked questions about how often he should report such a crime to the military police. And you prefaced your answer by saying that weren't a professional soldier and you can't say exactly what the procedure was within a given unit, depending on the position the commander had, and I'd just like to explore the basis for your answers a bit more. Now, again, in your evidence yesterday and today, you have explained your familiarity with the duty of members of state bodies generally to report crimes, and you said earlier today also that you had no specialised knowledge or training in the duties of commanders vis-a-vis their subordinates. So I'd like to ask you a similar question in respect of your knowledge of the relationship between HV commanders and the military police. In the note of your interview with the Prosecution, you explained that you didn't have any direct knowledge of the daily actions of the military police in their units. And this Chamber has received quite extensive evidence, including from a number of military police officials and military police officers, about the system of dual command and control and subordination --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object. I completely disagree on the characterisation of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The structure of command and control, I take it that without qualifying it, Ms. Gustafson, would do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, the Chamber has received extensive evidence about the system of dual command and control and subordination --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, the issue is --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I will rephrase. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The Chamber has received extensive evidence about the system of command and control and subordination that existed among military police units, HV commanders, and the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: My question for you is: Do you have any specialised knowledge of the structure and operation of this system of command and control and subordination?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not have any specialised knowledge, and I said as much yesterday and this morning. I only know the fact that military prosecutors and deputy military prosecutors were in direct communication with representatives of the 72nd and 73rd Military Police Battalion who covered the territory under the jurisdiction of the Split Military Prosecutor's Office. That they were in communication, above all, with the authorised officials or officers of the criminal investigation departments of these units, and I knew that these units were under the control of the military police administration in Zagreb. As for the other relationships between various military structures on the field, I don't know anything about them and don't want to go into them. I only know that some -- that I communicated only with the authorised officers of the criminal investigation sections of these units on cases that the Military Prosecutor's Office was seized of. I did not professionally communicate with others. There are special rules governing the work of the military police, and I'm sure that they contained all -- all the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And yesterday you were asked whether, in a situation where a commander has knowledge that the military police already knows about a particular crime, whether he has an additional duty to report it again to the military police. And your answer included the statement that: "If he knows the MP is already seized of the event, it would be pointless to report to them the same thing. However, the commander is duty-bound to help, together with his officers, to secure evidence and facts that might be helpful for the future proceedings." And I'd like to ask you a related but slightly different question which is, in a situation that a HV commander is aware that the military police knows about a particular crime committed by one of the commander's subordinates and the commander knows that the military police is not taking steps to ensure that that crime is investigated and punished, do you feel that you have a sufficient knowledge of the systems of command and control, subordination, and duties of HV commanders to tell the court whether the commander should take further steps to ensure that that subordinate is investigated and punished, and, if so, what those further steps might be. Do you think you have the knowledge and expertise to answer that question, and, if so, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can answer the question; at least according to what my understanding was at the time when I was deputy military prosecutor. In the situation as you presented it, the commander of a unit, where he becomes aware of a case being obstructed by the military police in relation to his subordinate, the commander should check on what steps are being taken with the higher -- with his superior officer in the military police hierarchy, or, rather, with the superior officer of the military police, and, if so, he should seek to be received and discuss the matter with the military prosecutor on the matter. At any rate, throughout the time, or at least initially, he should secure all the evidence and facts in order to enable the prosecution structures to deal with the case as best they can.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have D1631 brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'd like to move now, Mr. Bajic, to another topic, which is the memo or the list, I guess, that you provided to the -- your office provided to the Gotovina Defence relating to the status of a number of alleged killing incidents. And there's no cover memo or anything to this list so I'd just like to ask you if I'm correct in my understanding that you were provided with the list of 337 alleged killing victims listed in the clarification of the indictment to this case. Is that -- and you were asked to provide information in the possession of the state attorney on any investigation or prosecution into each of these incidents. Is that more or less what you were asked to do here?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear on your question. You have to explain what it is that you're referring to. Are you referring to the data contained in the table; or are you speaking in general terms?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm asking, yeah, what you were asked to do specifically in creating this table because the numbers in the chart correspond to the numbers in the clarification to the indictment in this case, and there are a total of 337 individuals listed in that clarification. Were you provided with that list of 337 individuals?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember at this time. I would have to look at both the query and the report. We did as we normally dealt with these matters, both when we received requests from the Defence or the Prosecution. I suppose we received this list of injured parties and then we checked the Prosecution archives against the information and then dealt with the matter. But I would have to check precisely to see whether these are the documents that I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, because the -- there are 88 victims or individuals listed in this chart and they're not, as you can see, they have numbers that start with 3, 5, 6, 7, but they are not sequential throughout the chart. And I'm wondering if you were provided with a larger list of names and that these were the 88 that you were able to find information about an investigation or prosecution on. Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot, because I don't have information on the matter. Certain individuals in my office did the job, and I can't explain why the sequential numbers were written as they were. What should be done in this case is to locate the request and everything else that was connected to that file.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look at the first entry, the case file number says KN-DO-5/07. Does that entry indicate that a case file into this incident was opened in 2007?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I take it that the same numbering system applies throughout the entries in this chart, whereby the last two digits of the case file indicate that -- the date that the case file was opened; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could look at entry number 7, Sava Babic, which is at the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This chart indicates that Mario Dukic was convicted for murder in relation to this incident. And in connection with that case, I'd like to look at 65 ter 7378, which is the case under tab 5, which I think you have already located in the bundle you have. The first document here is a judgement of the Split Military Court. And if we look at the first page lower down in the B/C/S and the bottom of the English, and moving on to the second page in the English, this indicates that the accused Mario Dukic a member of the 134th Home Guard Regiment is convicted for the killing of Petar Botar in Kolarina and sentenced to six years imprisonment. And if we go to the next page in English and the next page in the B/C/S as well. And if we move -- sorry. We can see that in the English and moving on to the next page in the B/C/S that the accused Mario Dukic as well as the other two co-accused are acquitted for the murder of Sava Babic. And if we can go to page 19 in the B/C/S and page 28 in the English, this is a later judgement of the Zadar County Court that confirmed these verdicts; namely the conviction of Mario Dukic for the killing of Petar Botar, as well as the acquittal of the other two accused for the murder of Sava Babic; is that right? [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So where the chart indicated that Mario Dukic had been convicted for the murder of Sava Babic that's not quite correct, I take it. It should have been noted that he was convicted for the murder of Petar Botar but acquitted for the murder of Sava Babic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If could I tender this case file 65 ter 7378, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2611.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2611 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go now to 65 ter 7377.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is the case that's under tab 4 in your bundle, Mr. Bajic. And this case relates to entry number 107 on the chart, which is the victim by the name of Manda Tizma [phoen]. And the entry states that the county court in Sibenik and the Supreme Court of the Republic of Croatia found that the accused Zeljko Sunjerga guilty for this killing and convicted him to a sentence of four years and 11 months.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we go to page 8 of the English and page 7 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd just like to confirm with you, Mr. Bajic, that this is the judgement of the Supreme Court of Croatia which did, indeed, convict Zeljko Sunjerga, who was at the time of the killing a member of the 15th Home Guard Regiment for this incident; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If could I tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2612.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to move to another topic, so if it suits the Court, perhaps we can take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will first have a break of 25 minutes, which means that we will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Ms. Gustafson, the Chamber would like to inform the parties about a decision taken on the application for eleven 92 bis statements to be admitted into evidence. The reasons will follow, but in order to expedite matters, the Chamber grants the request by the Defence to call the four out of the 11 witnesses for cross-examination, but the Chamber decided that, proprio motu, that we'll hear the cross-examination, the testimony given in cross-examination by those witnesses through videolink, limited time. The -- there will be limited time. We'd like to hear the testimony of those four witnesses in cross-examination on one day, just in a short sequence of, perhaps, 30 or 40 minutes. That's still to be determined. The Chamber will then decide on all 11 statements, whether or not to admit them into evidence. The Chamber expects that there's no further need for proofing these witnesses prior to them being examined, to them being cross-examining and if the parties consider that there would be any reason to further proof those witnesses, then the parties are invited, first, to inform the Chamber. The Chamber will then consider those reasons and see whether or not any orders should be issued in relation to that matter. That is -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I misspoke where I said that the request for cross-examination was a Defence request. It was a Prosecution request. That's the risk of doing it without a written text before me. Is this clear? The reason why we're giving this decision at this moment is because it may take some time for the -- for the Defence and the Registry to prepare for the cross-examination, and to have the assistance of the victims and witness sections to get the witnesses at the right place at the right time. If it causes any further practical problems, you're invited, first, to inform the Registry, and, if need be, there will be communication with the Chamber. Any questions in relation to this decision which, of course, will -- reasons will be given at a later stage. Then, Mr. Bajic, I apologise for -- well, not for wasting your time at least because you could have had a longer break and not be bothered by these kind of matters, although you're certainly familiar with the possibility that this happens now and then in courtrooms. Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to continue the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, I'd like to move to another topic, but, pardon me, just before I do that, you stated earlier that you couldn't remember the exact request you received that caused your office to create the chart we were looking at of investigations and prosecutions into individual alleged killing incidents. And I'm wondering if you would be willing to provide that request to the Prosecution so that we could -- and the parties and the Court, so we could better understand the basis for your chart. Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you were asked to describe factors that hindered the ability of the Croatian state authorities to investigate or prosecute the killing incidents listed in the clarification to the indictment in this case, and you described various problems such as witnesses or suspects being in other countries and weak cooperation with police and prosecuting bodies in those countries in the past. Now, the Chamber has received evidence that after Operation Storm a system of sanitation was set up and implemented, involving members of the MUP and HV, whereby corpses that were discovered in the liberated territory were collected by sanitation teams and buried in cemeteries, for the most part without an on-site investigation being conducted or any criminal report being filed. And yesterday you mentioned the 2001 exhumation at the Knin cemetery where many of these victims were buried. So I do understand that you are now aware of the existence of this sanitation system, even if you didn't know about it at the time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I learned after those disinterments started. This is what I learned subsequently. I repeat again, I did not work in that area at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think the question was unclear and so the answer is unclear. Was he aware of this sanitation system. I'm not sure if the witness now says he is aware of how sanitation was carried out or he is aware that bodies were buried and there was an exhumation in 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, could you further explore what exactly you were meaning and whether that is the same as the witness means when he is talking about the sanitation system.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, do I understand correctly that you now understand that there was a sanitation system implemented after Operation Storm in the manner I described?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, now, I learned of that subsequently. First information I received was after this major exhumation in Knin in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the fact that many of these individuals were simply buried without an on-site investigation being carried out or a criminal report being filed, that was another -- that is another quite significant factor that has delayed the investigation and prosecution of these incidents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I concur. Because only after 2001 or, better said, 2004, when first results of forensics examinations in that area become known, we determined the identity of 128 persons after whom 104 were determined to be killed at close range; 75 of them being killed around the time of the 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th August 1995 and the remainder of them were killed in the subsequent 30 days. This is what I remember from those documents from those case files. And on the basis of those examinations concerning the exhumations, we use such materials in the cases that are ongoing in the area of Sibenik and Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could move now to 65 ter 2273, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, this is a report from the HINA news agency from the 8th of February, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we move down the page in the English, there's a remark that is attributed to you. And in the third-last paragraph it says: "He," and this is referring to you, "said that since 2001, authorities have taken a more serious approach to investigating crimes committed by members of the Croatian army and the police, adding that this was important to the credibility of Croatia's judiciary." And then in the next paragraph it says, Bajic said that: "Fair and legal criminal proceedings could contribute to establishing the truth and help historians to give a final judgement." First, I'd like to ask you if you recall making that statement and if it accurately reflect what is you said.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was my speech at a conference in 2007 at the Sheraton Hotel, if I recall it correctly, attended by the participants whose words are reflected here. I agree with my statements in this press release except for the misquoted figures. If I may explain that, it may be useful for you. I know that this was so irrespective of what is written here. Up to 2002, we had registered some 4.000 people reported in the criminal justice system, not prosecuted but reported. Most of those cases were tried in absentia, even in some cases there were indictments. In 2002, I issued an instruction to all my public prosecutors to undertake a review of the cases dating from 1991 onwards, because I thought that a large number of cases were not processed as per the standards which are now obtaining in Croatian and international judiciary. Many people were processed for war crimes, although, based on the elements of the criminal offence, pursuant to Croatian law, those criminal offences were more of a character of armed rebellion, Croatia against the state, et cetera. So to cut a long story short, from 2001 to date, out of the total of slightly less than 4.000 persons, we have 1100 people prosecuted, the others, the other cases were dropped or abandoned or those criminal offences were re-qualified. So expect for those figures stated here, everything else reported here is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That you. Just to clarify the record, you're clarifying the figures in the paragraph above the ones that I read out; is it -- that's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I could seek some clarification on the last answer. You were talking about trials in absentia. Were they mainly conducted against Croat, Croatian defendants or -- Croat defendants or Serb defendants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Trials in absentia used to be conducted in Croatia until a couple of years ago when up to a point when I, as a prosecutor general, issued an instruction to my prosecutors to object to trials in absentia for the well-known reasons to all. Those proceedings were conducted mainly against the members of other armies. We did not keep records of their ethnic affiliations. But mainly these were members of the enemy combatants and mainly citizens of Serb nationality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And your remark about authorities since 2001 taking a more serious approach to investigating crimes committed by members of the Croatian army and the police, would that include crimes committed in the aftermath of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we -- oh, could I tender that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2613.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2613 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go now to 65 ter 4461, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, these are the minutes of a meeting -- the meeting of the 33rd Session of the council for cooperation with the ICTY. It was held on the 6th of November, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could scroll down in the English and then move to the next page in the English --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We can see at the top of the English page there that this was attended by a number of government -- Croatian government ministers and other senior officials in the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we go to the -- look at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S and move down in the English as well, we can see there's one agenda item, which is: "Defining the position of the Republic of Croatia on the proposal made by Attorney Rivkin in respect to the strategy of appearing before the MKS ICTY, in connection with the Oluja operation." And if we could go to the next page in the B/C/S and also the next page in the English. Participants discuss a -- or a number of proposals are discussed in relation to this strategy such as filing a case before the International Court of Justice against the FRY. And we see Dr. Granic speaks in the middle of the page, at the time the ministry of foreign affairs. He starts by saying that in his opinion, all the proposals seemed bad from a political point of view. And at the bottom of this paragraph he says: "Second of all, in defining the Oluja operation, we, ourselves, called it a military and police operation. So it was a planned operation, and it was executed as planned. Our shortcomings surfaced subsequently, after the Oluja operation, when we have not processed possible perpetrators of war crimes." And if we could go to the next page in the English and the bottom of the page in the B/C/S. And this is Mr. Separovic speaking who, at the time, was the director of the HIS. And he says that he "fully agreed with Dr. Granic that filing the case would not stop the Tribunal from investigating the Oluja operation ..." And if we move down the page in the English and go to the next page in the B/C/S where Mr. Penic speaks and he is, at the time, the minister of the interior. At the beginning of the second sentence he says: "Mr. Penic added that he deems that we are to blame for not penalising those who commit the crimes in the aftermath of the Oluja, but that the crimes were committed only by individuals or small groups of people. We must not forget that the suffering caused to the Republic of Croatia was a planned and organised crime committed by a state." And, finally, if we could go to page 5 of the English and the bottom of that same page in the B/C/S. These are the conclusions of Dr. Ramljak, who was then the minister of justice. And under point 2, it says: "Events that occurred after the Oluja operation. It seems that it is necessary to reassess the strategy taken two to three years ago related to not processing the events and crimes committed in the aftermath of the operation, but we need to keep in mind that the council for cooperation with ICTY and MKS is not obliged to discuss this issue."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you've -- you've stated that the Croatian authorities became more serious about prosecuting crimes committed after Operation Storm after 2001, and here, in November 1998, we have senior members of the Croatian government discussing the fact that crimes committed after Operation Storm have not been processed, and the minister of justice concluded that they should reassess the strategy related to not processing the events and crimes committed in the aftermath of Operation Storm. And my question is: Would you agree that under the regime of former President Tudjman that there was a reluctance on the part of the political leadership to investigate or process suspected HV crimes committed after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going objective on foundational grounds. Is it a general question or is she asking him specifically about a comment in the document? In that case, I would ask for foundation as to what this witness knows about what the comment refers to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's a general question, Your Honour, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- I think the foundation has been laid from the witness's position and remarks on the nature of these investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think, as a matter of fact, it was only, as Mr. Misetic said, in that case I would ask for a foundation that if it is not a general question. Let's first hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just so it is on the record, he has been shown documents but the question is not related to the documents that he's been shown. In other words, not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not necessarily distinct from but not focussing on documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On it's document, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question, Ms. Gustafson, so that we're ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, my question was: Would you agree that under the regime of former President Tudjman, there was a reluctance on the part of the political leadership to investigate or process suspected HV crimes committed after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to this question, I can say as follows: First of all, we have to go back to the fact concerning my job during the Operation Storm and later up to 2001 and 2002. At the time in question, I was deputy military prosecutor until the end of 1996. After that, I was deputy county prosecutor in Split. In 2000, I was county prosecutor in Split; and in 2002, I become prosecutor general of the Republic of Croatia. When I say Croatian authorities decided this or that, well, when I came to the post of prosecutor general, I conducted an analysis of all the cases, together with my associates. I analysed what has been done up to that point. In respect to that, I think that in many cases things took a wrong turn. I was against trials in absentia. I believe that in many cases indictments were too wide, and in many cases crimes have not been prosecuted, and I still believe that. Based on that, I issued written instructions and there's a written record of that and the Court can have them. Those instructions were to public prosecutors on how to review the present cases or the cases at the time and -- but also to seek from police anything of evidence for the cases that had not been processed. As a prosecutor, I can talk about that. I cannot offer any political assessment on the opinions and positions taken by some member of the political leadership, because I do not have any immediate knowledge of that other than what I read off the screen right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know why the Croatian authorities waited until 2001, six years after the events in question, to begin exhuming individuals from the Knin cemetery in a situation where the MUP at least knew where these people were buried and the fact that no on-site investigation had been carried out because it was, in fact, MUP officials involved in their burial. Do you know why it took until 2001 to begin exhuming these bodies and carrying out autopsies?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. What I know, since I became prosecutor general that on several occasions I launched initiatives to the minister of police and other participants who could jointly collect facts relevant for detection of perpetrators of war crimes to step up their efforts to establish departments for war crimes, to adopt team-work approach, to investigate at the levels of county prosecutors offices in all counties, particularly those in the areas of Vukovar, Osijek, Zadar, and Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that this time delay before the exhumations were carried out was a factor that has affected the ability to investigate and prosecute these cases. On top of that simple delay of time, the fact that these bodies were in the ground decomposing for six years, that's a further factor that has hindered the investigations; is that right? The fact that the bodies had been decomposing for six years and evidence had -- potential forensic evidence had been lost due to decomposition. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The passage of time, as is known by everybody in this courtroom, plays into the hand of the perpetrator and hinders those who want to identify the perpetrators and prosecute criminal offences. Unfortunately, this is true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bajic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At this time, I would like to tender the charts that were circulated earlier. I believe we have agreement with the Gotovina Defence, which are 65 ter 7381 and 7382.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 7381 becomes Exhibit P2614; and 65 ter number 7382 will become Exhibit P2615.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is usually not aware of 65 ter numbers. We're talking about which charts exactly?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I believe they were sent to the Chamber this morning by e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This morning by e-mail. Let me check. Yes, it is kind of an extract, and agreed upon between the parties. P2614 and P2615 are admitted into evidence. Mr. Misetic, any reason to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. Bajic. Just I have a few questions for you to clarify a few matters. You've testified on questioning by the Prosecutor about the requirement -- you were asked about whether a commander has a duty to file a criminal report with the Military Prosecutor's Office. And my question to you is: If the commander informs the military police of a criminal act, has he fulfilled his obligations under the Criminal Procedure Code?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Criminal reports are primarily sent and submitted to law enforcement organisations, be it civilian or military police. I answered this question in this way today, if a commander reports something to military police, he has discharged his obligation pursuant to the Criminal Procedure Act, particularly if concurrently with that he has secured the evidence, provided all the information to the detection and prosecution authorities which are necessary to successfully the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, but the first -- let me ask you, under the military criminal justice system, which institution has the primary responsibility of detecting crime within the military and securing relevant evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this topic was discussed at length in direct examination. I don't see how it arises from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If it is clear and the Prosecution agrees with what the witness just answered, then I won't proceed further. If it is still this dispute, I think it needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact, the matter was dealt with in examination-in-chief, then Ms. Gustafson asked questions to the witness on what a commander would have to do if he had knowledge that the military police, although aware of the crime, did not -- well, let's say seriously investigate the matter or investigate the matter, and the answer of the witness was that under those circumstances, a commander had to either seek a hierarchical higher person to trigger such an investigation, and if this would not result in an investigation, that, under those circumstances, he would have to address the military prosecutor. I see the witness is nodding yes. This summarises the more detailed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That was not issue I was dealing with. I was actually dealing with his testimony from yesterday, not today, where he talked about filing of criminal reports with the Military Prosecutor's Office, and I will pull it up right now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we come to the objection of Ms. Gustafson. How does this arise from cross-examination? You now refer to what he testified yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In -- the first very limited part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So, again, Mr. Bajic, the question was: Who has the primary responsibility under the military criminal justice system at the time for uncovering crime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, could you give us the reference, the page reference of yesterday's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or a few words which allows us to use WordWheel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will have it. Just one moment, Mr. President. Page 20798, beginning at line 26 [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, my problem is that page 20798 has 25 lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's at least my ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll give you the sentence then. The question was: "And more generally if a military commander ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Generally. 16 ... same page line 16?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise for the error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "And more generally if a military court ..." That's on line 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question is again: Who has the fundamental responsibility under the military criminal justice system for uncovering crime?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces of law enforcement, which include the civilian and military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, once a commander forwarded information to the military police that a crime was committed by an unknown member of the HV, are you aware of whether, as a matter of practice, the military police ever reported back to the commander about the results of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, although I believe that, under the rules governing the profession, they should have reported back. They should have forwarded the criminal report to the Military Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, no. Maybe -- I just want to make sure we're not talking past each other. My question wasn't whether under the rules they should have reported to the Military Prosecutor's Office. The question was: Would they report back to the commander about what they had done in the investigation of the criminal offence; and if your answer is yes, you've cited to rules governing the profession, can you tell us what rules specifically you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was not aware of what the military police did, in relation to those who had filed a report or given notice to it. But under these standards, it is only natural that you should report back to the party submitting a report about what was done upon the report, just as the prosecutor's office, upon receiving a report, would inform the reporting party on what was done.
