I'm drawing a parallel there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- you're referring to the standards and this is at page 48, line 17 of the transcript. What standards are you referring to? Are you referring to specific written standards or are you speaking about general practices?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the general practice above all, because I don't know what the rules governing the military police specifically say in relation to this procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then my question to you is: Do you believe you are very familiar with the general practice of the military police in 1995 with respect to whom it was reporting information to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you were asked a question about commanders conducting investigations parallel with a criminal investigation. And I wanted to just --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify that that was commanders conducting disciplinary investigations, just so there is no confusion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Commanders conducting a disciplinary investigation parallel with a criminal investigation. My question to you is: Did you understand that a commander would conduct or could conduct a -- an investigation into a criminal act under the umbrella of a disciplinary investigation at the same time that the military police and the Military Prosecutor's Office were conducting their own investigation into that criminal act?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What would the disciplinary investigation -- can you explain, when you say "Theoretically speaking, yes," as a matter of practice, was that the practice at the time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I don't know what the practice was like. But if a criminal report was filed for a serious crime, then it was a superfluous matter to engage in a disciplinary procedure as well, but, of course, it depended on the commander and the commander's inclination toward investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you were asked -- you were shown some documents from a court file, and it related to individuals in the Golubic area who were arrested by the military police and prosecuted for looting. And you were asked the question, first, whether you believed that looting was to some extent permitted or accepted in the HV. And my question to you is if could you explain that your answer to that question if, in fact, the military police arrested these individuals and were put on trial, can you further explain your answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could just clarify again. The question was permitted or accepted within HV units, not within the HV generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And military police, I believe, the question said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's check what we believe what the question says. Could you take us to the relevant --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will take it, but I'm certain that Ms. Gustafson said by letting members --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's not pronounce ourselves on what you certainly think she said. Let's first look at the transcript and if there's any reason to -- for doubt whether the transcript expresses exactly what Ms. Gustafson said, we can verify that, rather than to, in the presence of the witness, tell what your recollection is, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now at page 15, beginning at line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. 15/17. One second.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The question begins at line 25 of page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, the question begins at line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second. I will slowly read to the witness the portion of the transcript you want to draw his attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It starts then -- the specific portion is the reference to the 72nd Military Police Battalion which is part of the question, which is within line 21.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was a reference, a specific reference to an individual who is -- who it was under indictment and became a member of the 72nd Military Police Battalion. That was part of the question that related to a specific fact in the judgement. The actual question begins at line 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just -- the question is introduced by a reference to the portions of the files read to the witness. I'll just read both the introduction and then the question. Mr. Bajic, I read from the transcript of this morning the following. Ms. Gustafson said: "Now, having read these files and based on your experience as a prosecutor and as a military prosecutor at the time of these events, would you agree that these cases contain indications, and I'm referring specifically to indications such as large group of HV soldiers loading looted items onto trucks in Knin, a soldier under indictment for theft becoming a member of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, and a large group of conscripts loading looted items onto a truck in front of their unit command. Do these indications indicate that, to you, looting was, to some extent, accepted or permitted within HV units at the time." That was the question which was put to you and you started your answer by saying: "I absolutely agree with your conclusion." Mr. Misetic wants to put a question to you in relation to this question and answer. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, my question is -- that was your answer. In light of the fact though that this information comes from a situation where these perpetrators were arrested by the military police and put on trial for it, can you explain why you would absolutely agree that you -- looting was, to some extent, accepted or permitted within the HV units at the time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, from the case files that were presented to me, these were cases 1, 2, 3, that's how they were designated when I got them. It follows undoubtedly from them that the theft or whatever you want to term it, by members of the Croatian army in the civilian buildings in the area, was widespread and this is something that follows from the indictments. It is true that the military police, in these very three cases, did react and filed criminal reports. It is also true that these three cases saw the perpetrators processed and convicted. However, the fact of the matter is that thefts like these, which were not processed and which we knew had happened, had been far more in numbers. Such statements were made in, among others, judgements themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then to follow up on this, you were also asked some questions about the applicability of the amnesty law to these particular cases, and you said in a response to a question by the Presiding Judge that these crimes would not have been covered by the amnesty, because they wouldn't have been considered connected with the war. The judgement came down in 1998. I noted that the indictment alleged that the theft took place on 8th of September, 1995. Are you aware of - and I don't believe it is disputed in this case - what military operation involving units of the Split Military District began on the 8th of September, 1995; and you are aware where that military operation was taking place on that date?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether this was Operation Maestral or something like that, that I heard from the media. But this stems from my general knowledge and not my knowledge in the capacity of a prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If whatever these individuals were doing was connected with or related to Operation Maestral, would it have fallen under the amnesty act and, therefore, would not have been prosecuted in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Law on General Amnesty has been well explained by me, I believe. Looting and theft cannot be connected with the war, and this is more than clear and I speak as a prosecutor now. What is connected to the war as collateral event is something quite different, and cannot, in any way, be related to looting, and, therefore, cannot be subject to the Law on General Amnesty. At least that is my view of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll just check your answer. It was interpreted as that you said -- I'm sorry, interpreted that this event cannot, in any way, be related to ... Related to what?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To war operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Bajic, you were asked questions about the processing of crime, and one of the questions put to you was that there were only five criminal reports filed in August and September 1995 against members of the HV and that chart is now Exhibit P2614.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify, it was five criminal reports filed in August and September against members of the HV for crimes relevant to this indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, we will flip through some of these pages which I admittedly don't have in front of me. For example, if we could go to page 8 in the English, please. I think there is only an English, actually. Now, you'll see in the grey these are the entries that the Prosecution believes are relevant to the indictment. The yellow ones are -- the grey entries, are those entries that relate to crimes committed in the liberated territories and in the specific municipalities which are the subject of this case. But you should know that the entire liberated area in Sector South is not subject to the Prosecution's case. The yellow entries indicate crimes perpetrated by HV members against -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Maybe I'm on the wrong page. Let me -- I guess I have to check with the Prosecution. I apologise for speaking mid-sentence. I'm looking at a version that was circulated that has entries 798 at the top in yellow, and I wondering whether the latest version has been uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We can check on that. I -- I have to check. I'm sorry. It just got uploaded, so I will check right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You'll have to take my word for it that, for example, entry 798 relates to a crime committed in the newly liberated area. It is Zelengrad, as you can see; but Zelengrad technically, although formally occupied territory on the crimes committed by HV, and the crime is against Serbs or Serb property doesn't technically fall within this chart. So my first question -- and if we can scroll to another page. If we can go to page 23, please. The grey area are, again, limited to the Prosecution's case in chief. The two white areas appearing on your screen right now are also crimes committed in the newly liberated areas. The question is: The relevant reports, for example, looking at number 12. Can you tell us the procedure -- the report, it is one report but it has five persons identified. The reports themselves contain multi-perpetrators in many cases. Is that consistent with your recollection of how the system functioned?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they are interconnected in terms of the manner of perpetration then they would be in one report if they committed the crime together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: By my count, and I'm just asking you whether this is consistent -- this chart --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I think your last question was more or the less the obvious. If under one number we have five names, then it means that under that number five names are reported. Now I take it that the witness has not calculated with him to see -- isn't this a matter of evaluation of what we find here? Because I already understand that you would say that there were far more persons reported or represented and that's a matter of one plus one makes two, and five plus five makes ten. Should we bother the witness with this or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm leading to the ultimate point, which is I'm going put the question that was put to him about a reluctance to prosecute and that was put, and I want to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness said that he couldn't express himself on the reluctance to prosecute. He said what he tell us what they did and he could not interpret acts or approaches or attitudes of the political leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I wasn't going to ask him about the political leadership. I was asking him about his office limited to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but, of course, there was no question about reluctance to prosecuted within his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The question was: Was there a reluctance to prosecute among the Tudjman regime, and that would be directly relevant to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, political leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- was specifically mentioned there, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We can look at the question again. This is at page 42, line 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 42, line 4. One second please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry you're right, Mr. President. It says political leadership. But ... as a technical matter, that reluctance would have to play out because the question is: Was there a reluctance on the part of the political leadership to investigate or prosecute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the witness said he could not tell us about what the political leadership and he then -- I certainly remember that. He said what he did. And, at the end, because I thought he was not answering the question he said: "I could not comment on but I cannot offer any political assessment on the opinions or positions taken by some members of the political leadership." So the question was about reluctance in the political leadership and the witness said that he couldn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. May I ask him then whether in working as a prosecutor he ever felt any reluctance by anyone who may have been in a political position not to prosecute? Because these events would say have been prosecuted by him or the offices he was working in, and I would just like to confirm that if such an allegation is going to be made at the end that the person who would have had to feel that reluctance, whether he felt it or didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it was implicit in his answer, I would say when he said that, but please correct me, Mr. Bajic, when I'm wrong. I under understood your answer to be that you did your job the way you thought you should do it and that you had no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- no signs of reluctance from the political leadership that reached you which you could comment on as far as whether there was such reluctance, yes or no, and these questions were based mainly on reading of this report of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. I will move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bajic. The next question is about the sanitation measures. You were asked a few questions about that. You've testified during your testimony here over the course of two days that you obviously are conducting examinations -- I'm sorry, investigations into these killing incidents. On the issue of how sanitation measures were carried out, have you found that the -- or evidence that the way that bodies were buried in Operation Storm was intended to cover up crime?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I cannot answer the question in relation to this specific issue, because the exhumations at Knin, which had to do with the earlier sanitisation processes, all the general information about the numbers of persons recovered there, the numbers of persons who were identified in the meantime and the findings of the identification, I have no additional information to what I just told you, save for the fact that certain corpses were identified. That's all the facts I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but, Mr. Misetic -- Mr. Bajic -- the first question we have to put to Mr. Bajic in this respect is: Did you investigate the practice or system or background of the sanitation that took place in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that if you do not find anything, if you are not looking for something, to find out what happened, Mr. Misetic, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand your point, Mr. President. That's why I had gotten up on my feet before when the question was posed and perhaps there is some confusion, and my computer is now down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, your question was highly suggestive to the extent that the focus of any investigation was not exclusively on trying to obtain evidence in relation to the human remains that were found but that it was also focussing on and investigating the way in which the sanitation was done in 1995, which, from what I understand from witness now, was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I may just have one minute, Mr. President. This is, again, I think discussed earlier today, and I just want to make sure that I'm clear on the witness's position. So if we could -- just one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you find the relevant transcript passage, please give us the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is at page 34, beginning with my comment at line 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to cut matters short. You told us that you learned subsequently when the exhumations had started that people had been buried without on-site investigations being conducted. That's people were buried under what was called by Ms. Gustafson as a sanitation system or perhaps a sanitation practice. Now, you told us that you learned about that only at a later stage. What Mr. Misetic is exploring now is whether, on from that moment, when you learned about the sanitation system, whether you explored and have drawn conclusions on why and how this sanitation system came into practice. Mr. Misetic, I think that's what you are trying to explore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the question, first of all, is: Did you investigate, did you explore, did you reach any conclusions in respect of the way in which this sanitation system was created, developed, background, why it was done this way? Did you explore that, did you make any findings in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally have no knowledge about that, any knowledge. The country prosecutor's office of Sibenik is seized of this case. They took part in the exhumation and by reviewing their case and gaining insight into it, I could have given you a specific answer to all your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they would have further explored that specific aspect, but apparently the witness doesn't know, Mr. Misetic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On the subjects of exhumations, you were asked questions about why exhumations began only in 2001. Do you recall at whose request the exhumations were done in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you involved in the exhumations in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2001, I was with the Public Prosecutor's Office in Split. The exhumation was at Knin, which is part of the Sibenik Public Prosecutor's Office, which is outside of my jurisdiction which I'm trying repeatedly to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you know why 2001 was the year that exhumations began? What was the factual basis which caused exhumations to begin in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The witness was already asked this question, and he said quite clearly that he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic is phrasing the question slightly differently because he would very much like to have the answer. Well, you've heard the question now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer is clear. The witness says, I do not know. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness said, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is my mistake, not to wait for the interpretation, but I'm afraid that this is the result of many, many years in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You were asked -- you were shown an article from HINA, which had a quote from you, quoting you as saying that a more serious approach to investigation began after 2001. And I just wanted to ask you to explain the comment. Was it a less serious approach prior to 2001?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In trying to provide an answer to this question, I said, after I came to the post of public prosecutor general of Croatia, I was of opinion that a serious review of all war crimes had to be done. Those up to the point. Analysing the type and number of cases, I established that in a certain segment the scope was too broad, that there was a large number of trials in absentia, and, on the other hand, that a large number of criminal offences had not been detected and processed; and for that reason I sought from all county prosecutors who were in charge of the operations in the field to organise a system within their prosecutor's offices, in such a way, to strengthen their departments dealing with war crimes to coordinate their work with police and intelligence services, and by doing so, try to obtain as much evidence as possible to enable them to process those cases that had not been processed that far. On the other hand, I also issued an instruction whereby trials in absentia should not be allowed to happen from that point onwards and also in the pending cases for them to reassess whether the indictments had been drafted up to scratch, up to the standards that had been elevated on the basis of knowledge, know-how, experience, information, to reassess whether the criminal offences were really war crimes and not less serious offences; and at the same time I was facing the facts that it was exceptionally difficult to collect information about war crimes that had occurred ten years prior to that date. I launched an initiate to strengthen institutional cooperation with other prosecutors general in the region to facilitate the acquisition of evidence from other countries and evidence from the archives of this Tribunal. All this is -- led to a fact that the number of earlier cases dropped from almost 4.000 to 1100 and that, on the other hand, we launched a host of new cases and that we referred number of cases to other countries in the region, where people residing there were prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bajic, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, any further questions? I also just check as we usually do, whether my colleagues or whether I have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Kinis has one or more questions for you Mr. Bajic. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, I wanted to ask you one question regarding war booty because we had a lot of evidences that HV commanders issued orders -- not orders or instructions which allowed to collect some sort of war booty for military needs. Did you ever receive any instruction which, in legal sense, explained what war booty was? During your business as a military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And did you distinguish these incidents where collection of home appliances, households were conducted in organised manner by militaries, and -- and separate such incidents and treated differently?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in the same manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, I -- I have one question in relation to the statement you gave to -- to the Gotovina Defence. You said in paragraph 4 that the military prosecutor, they wore uniforms but were, in fact, acting entirely within the system of the public prosecutor. What you say, at least that's how I understood it, they are not soldiers but they were wearing military uniforms. Did you wear a uniform yourself?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did wear a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What -- I mean, was this a fancy uniform or were you a member some unit or -- I mean, could you choose your own insignia or what -- could you explain to us what uniform you were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the decrees were enacted at the end of 1991 on the organising of the military justice system, the minister of defence, at the proposal of the prosecutor general of Croatia, deployed the existing deputy prosecutors from the existing prosecuting services or offices into military prosecutor services. And in 1992, on the 6th of February, I changed the label on my door. I put military -- deputy military prosecutor instead of public prosecutor and wore a uniform, which I received together with the decision on my deployment. But the military prosecution service was part of the prosecution service of the Republic of Croatia. The second instance body that we reported to, who took decisions on our decisions, was the republican prosecution service or the central prosecution service of the Republic of Croatia. While we wore the uniforms well, first of all, we received our wartime deployment papers, and we wore them, because it was inconceivable as per the standards obtaining at the time, for military personnel to be prosecuted and tried by people not wearing uniforms, not being military personnel. Of course, this has been abandoned since. I wore the uniform until the expiry of my term of office on the 6th of December, 1996. Apart from the technical support that we received from the Ministry of Defence, we had no other obligations or duties towards the Ministry of Defence. None whatsoever. Moreover, second instances decisions on first instances decisions of military courts were done by the county court in Split, for instance, for criminal offences punishable by a certain number of years, and up above that threshold the second instances decision on county court decision was done by the Supreme Court of Croatia. As far as our salaries are concerned, we received them from the Ministry of Justice because we are part of that justice system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you said in order to present an authority over the soldiers of the Croatian army, was that exclusively then within your office? Is that how I have to understand it? That if suspects would -- or if -- if other persons, or did you also go into the field and ...

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we wore military uniforms, both prosecutors and military judges, during our term of office in the military justice system. As far as going out into the field, those consisted of going at crime scenes or reconstructions and these were the only outings that we had as military prosecutors wearing uniforms. We did not take part in regular activities or operations or actions of the HV because we were deployed within the Military Prosecutor's Office or we deployed as part of the military justice system. We had the status of a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, again, could you describe from your insignia which unit you belonged to, which -- although I do understand that it was not in any way functional, but what unit were you a member of when you wore that uniform?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not members of any unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what could other people think you would be a member of, looking at your uniform?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could not tell us apart from regular soldiers, because there was no indication on the uniform to that effect. Maybe towards the end, in 1996, but at the very beginning there were no insignia telling us, military judges or military prosecutors, apart from regular soldiers. We were deployed by a decision of the minister of defence at the initiative and proposal of the prosecutor general. This is written in the decrees that have been already been tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what rank, according to your uniform?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any rank for the first couple of years, but in 1995 or 1996, towards the end, I was given a rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Different subject, so we leave the dress to impress behind us. This very special confidential register, you said that existed with only a few entries and nothing remaining in that register, what would one need to end up in this register? I mean, what was so special about it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic registers for the operation of public prosecutors are those that we discussed in great detail when cross-examined by the Prosecutor. However, in public prosecutor's service and in the military prosecutor service, as per the regulations which applied to both service, they were identical. There were some registers with different degrees of confidentiality. What was entered into those registers were memoranda, letters or information coming from other state bodies which classified their missives, and because of the rules then and which are applied still now, the state body which receives a classified document should not change its status without the approval of the author or the sender of such classified document. In specific cases, several cases, in my opinion mistakenly, this is the only way I can explain that, ended up in the so-called VT or very confidential register. But when there was established that there were criminal reports, they were transferred or re-entered into the KT register and processed. So no special secrets lay behind that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everything in this special registers finally ended up in one of the ordinary registers. I'm trying to find out whether there was any information --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of a very sensitive nature which was finally not finding its way to the ordinary registers. I can imagine high-ranking suspects or very specific crimes, corruption, whatever. I'll just trying to find out whether there was anything in those registers which would be different from what we finally find in the regular registers.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that was material and relevant for a criminal report, which means if information contained in a confidential document ended up in the regular KT register and processed. And as far as can I tell you, this happened in Split. Certain things had to be registered in the VT register if it was necessary to keep them confidential, so that the process -- processing be successful ultimately, and it was necessary only for a handful of people to be aware of such information to successfully conclude a case. We went through those registers to use any information which was necessary to successfully prosecute some recent cases but nothing remained in those VT registers as closed cases. I mentioned this yesterday, because I noticed that some prosecutors - for instance that in Sibenik - re-- mistakenly entered a case into a VT register instead of the KT register, and out of an abundance of caution, I mentioned that so that you get the full information. And this was the only reason why I mentioned it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Have the questions by the Bench triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I just have two very minor procedural matters to raise, but we don't need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In relation to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In relation to the witness but he doesn't need to be present for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One other question, Ms. Gustafson, yesterday you said you would consider whether you would need more time. Is there anything remaining there or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Bajic, this then concludes your testimony in this court. Being a witness certainly is not the same as being a prosecutor in court; I'm aware of that. I would like to thank you very much for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I would like to wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Bajic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, it's 20 minutes to 1.00. There are a few procedural matters which the Chamber would like to raise today. If the matters you would like to raise in relation to this witness could wait until after the break, that would be appreciated, and it may save time for the coming days if we could deal with those procedural matters after the break. We'll resume at five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few procedural items on the agenda. Let's start with the first one. Ms. Gustafson, you said you had two matters in relation to Mr. Bajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first is P2614, which was one of the summary charts that was just admitted into evidence. A mistake was made. A version had been sent out last night. I had further discussions with Mr. Misetic, a further version was then sent out this morning. We then made a mistake and uploaded the incorrect version. As Mr. Misetic noted in his re-direct, that has been now corrected with the helpful assistance of the Registrar. So the correct version is now in e-court under P2614. And the other matter was that I neglected to tender 65 ter 4461, which were the minutes of the coordination council from the 6th of November, 1998, and I'd ask that that be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, any objections against 65 ter 4461?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President. I -- I will note that with respect to that document, I will seek a stipulation from the Prosecution about one fact, but we'll do that at a late date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2616.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2616 is admitted into evidence. Ms. Gustafson, I made a comment yesterday on some columns in a document, where I had some problems to -- to find that the English and the original was the same DO, DOD, has that been resolved?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the translation has been created and an e-mail explaining the error was sent to the Chamber yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has not yet been transferred to us. But Defence is aware of that as well. So, therefore, that matter has been resolved. Then I would like to move to my next item, which is a statement from this Chamber with regard to the expert report of witness Ivan Pokaz. On the 9th of July of this year, the Gotovina Defence filed the expert report of Witness Pokaz, of which the final translation was communicated to the Chamber by e-mail on the 15th of July, 2009. The curriculum vitae of Witness Pokaz was subsequently filed on the 16th of July, 2009. On the 10th of August, 2009, the Prosecution filed its notice, pursuant to Rule 94 bis, of the Rules, objecting to the report and challenging the expertise and qualifications of the witness. The Prosecution argued that the report should not be admitted into evidence. The Prosecution moreover indicated that, whether or not the Chamber would decide to admit the report, it would not seek to cross-examine the witness, unless he would be called to testify viva voce. On the 12th of August, 2009, the Markac Defence filed its notice, expressing its wish to cross-examine Witness Pokaz. On the 25th of August, 2009, the Gotovina Defence filed an addendum to the report -- to the expert report of Witness Pokaz, which elaborates on the use of quotation marks throughout the expert report. The Chamber defers its decision on admission of the expert report until after the testimony of Witness Pokaz. The Prosecution has in its notice made detailed challenges to the report, and the Chamber finds that the concerns of the Prosecution are not without merit. In particular, the Chamber has concerns in relation to the transparency of the methods applied by the witness and of the sources upon which the witness's conclusions are based, and in this regard, the Chamber emphasises that an expert is expected to give his expert opinion in full transparency of the established or assumed facts he relies upon and of the methods used when applying his knowledge, experience, or skills to form his expert opinion. The sources used in support of any expert opinion must be clearly indicated and accessible. If such transparency is lacking, this will seriously affect the parties' and the Chamber's possibility to test or challenge the factual basis on which the expert report -- on which the expert witness reached his or her conclusions, and thereby to assess the probative value of the expert report. The result might be non-admission or that only limited weight can be attached to the expert report. Therefore, before deciding on admission of the expert report, the Chamber will allow the parties, taking into account the mentioned guidance, to explore the opinions expressed by Witness Pokaz in his report. And this concludes the Chamber's statement. I add to this that leave is granted to the Prosecution to exceed the word limit as requested in the notice. I move to next item on the -- on my agenda, and we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. There is an issue still pending, in relation to the European Union Monitoring Mission. The Chamber would like to be informed by the Gotovina Defence on which documents are still missing. The Chamber has received and it has been filed, I think, a letter written by Mr. Solana, dated 13th of August. In the attachment to this letter, we find three categories of documents, the first documents which were received by the Prosecution - I think there are two - received by the Prosecution which were then later redacted by the EU and given back to the Prosecution for disclosure to the Defence. The second category in the attachment is those documents that could not be found in a new review of the archives. And then the third category was documents that apparently -- redacted documents were delivered on a certain date to the Gotovina Defence. I think it was the 1st of July, if I'm not mistaken. Does that mean, Mr. Misetic, that those documents were received directly from European Union Monitoring Mission or the European Union on that date and not through the Prosecution, as was the case with other documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is correct. We travelled to Brussels and picked up the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. These were six documents from what I understand. The Chamber will consider whether and how to proceed. An application is still made in this respect by the Defence, but the Chamber would like to be informed about what documents are now still sought by the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, we will certainly work on that expeditiously and get you a list. I want to be transparent, however that -- in addition to the documents that the Chamber narrowed the issues down to, we, in all likelihood will request from the Chamber a reconsideration on the issue of one category of documents which are the ECMM logs from RC Knin in Knin; and, therefore, there will be that additional set of documents. We have good faith basis to believe that they existed and that they would be highly relevant in this proceeding, so we will add that in addition to the list that has been -- the narrowing of the documents done by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether we narrowed. We invited, first, to focus on the documents for which, in this year of its existence, were available to the Chamber. And from the answer by Mr. Solana, we see that they have reviewed their archives in relation to those documents. Of course, this whole procedure is -- is a bit blurred here and there by documents sought, already available, or other documents considered to be in existence, which there is still doubt as to whether they do exist or not. So if we could get an update on -- on what you are still seeking, and if there are any further indications of the existence of such documents, of course, we would welcome that as well, so that we have a -- an update as to the present position. This is not in any way a commitment of the Chamber, other than that it will then seriously consider whether, and how, to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. These were the items on my agenda. Any further procedural matters? Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There was an issue with the exhibit list that we have received for experts Jones and experts Corn, and there are some documents listed there that have not been dealt with in the report. For Expert Corn, for example, we're talking about P1125, General Gotovina's order for attack; D1205, Mr. Rajcic's attachment for artillery; and P461, the Brioni transcript. And the issue, Mr. President, is that we have not received any notice as to what the opinion that is being sought by the expert on these documents is. We don't even know, based on the report, whether he was provided those documents, and if he weren't he is then going to be elicited opinions on the stand, we will not have proper notice of those documents. The same documents also have been on the exhibit list for Expert Jones, who is not listed as an artillery expert; and, therefore we object to those as well and I just want to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the opinions of the -- the experts are contained in their reports as the Chamber can see. With regard to the other documents that could potentially be employed, we have given that list of documents to the Prosecution. And we're simply following the procedure that the Prosecution employed in the direct examination of Colonel Konings, for instance, where we received a plethora of documents in addition to -- that had not been in his report that they used during the course of their direct examination. But the opinions that he -- that these experts are going to employ are in the actual report. There's not going do be any divergence from those opinions. We are simply giving the array of documents that could potentially come up during direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think one of the concerns expressed by Mr. Hedaraly is also whether these documents had been available to the expert when forming his opinion. And perhaps, ver briefly, I earlier read a statement with regard to the expert report of Mr. Pokaz and, of course, much of what was said in this statement might also apply to these expert reports. That is, the transparency and sources, assumed facts, of course, sometimes we find them, as far as Mr. Corn is concerned, for example, what facts he was given to base part of his opinion upon is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Those item had been -- the factual items with regard to Corn and with regard to anything that -- that was of a factual nature has been provided to counsel. So there has been, for instance, with Professor Corn, there was a series of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, of course, I think one of the concerns of Mr. Hedaraly is that he might have a full overview of all the material which was provided to or was available to the expert. And, of course, it might not always be easy to -- to have a complete overview and we have received submissions by the parties on whether there are any obligations in this respect. We have not decided on that matter or we have not given any orders, but we're working on it hard, where it seems that Defence is primarily looking at the matter from a point of view of disclosure obligations; whereas, the Prosecution's concerns seem to go more into the direction of how to test the evidence if we don't have that information. I'm not going to say anything further on it, but the Chamber expects soon to give further guidance and/or orders to the parties in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may just add one other issue. When the Chamber is considering the obligations in this regard, I would ask the Chamber to look at Mr. Konings report where, in fact, he cited two documents in his report. And in conjunction with that, we were provided any number of additional documents in a list provided by Mr. Russo that were provided to the witness -- to the expert, Colonel Konings. So the situation is clearly not dissimilar. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, what you are doing is you are opening arguments on the matter. What Mr. Hedaraly did is that he did put a certain matter on the record not really arguing the matter at this very moment. We -- the Chamber is, of course, in possession of the positions taken by the parties on what obligations there are. The parties are, meanwhile, in relation to the Pokaz report, aware of -- of what the Chamber needs to finally test of factual basis and to assess the probative value of expert reports.
